elements.quote: This living review aims to critically appraise available data about secondary attack rates from people with asymptomatic, pre-symptomatic and symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection.
elements.reason: The abstract identifies the work as a “living review,” but it does not explicitly use the term “systematic review” in the provided abstract text.

elements.quote: Purpose: This living review aims to critically appraise available data about secondary attack rates from people with asymptomatic, pre-symptomatic and symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection.
elements.reason: A clear main objective/review aim is stated under “Purpose.”

elements.quote: Study selection: Studies that report on contact tracing of index cases with SARS-CoV-2 infection in either English or Chinese were included.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an explicit inclusion criterion (and at least one eligibility criterion) via the “Study selection” statement.

elements.quote: Data sources: Medline, EMBASE, China Academic Journals full-text database (CNKI), and pre-print servers were searched from 30 December 2019 to 3 July 2020 using relevant MESH terms.
elements.reason: Information sources and the search date range (“from 30 December 2019 to 3 July 2020”) are reported.

elements.quote: Data extraction: Two authors independently extracted data and assessed study quality and risk of bias.
elements.reason: The abstract states that risk of bias was assessed (by two authors).

elements.quote: Data synthesis: Of 927 studies identi fi ed, 80 were included. Summary secondary attack rate estimates were 1% (95% CI 0% e 2%) with a prediction interval of 0% e 10% for asymptomatic index cases in ten studies, 7% (95% CI 3% e 11%) with a prediction interval of 1% e 40% for pre-symptomatic cases in 11 studies and 6% (95% CI 5% e 8%) with a prediction interval of 5% e 38% for symptomatic index cases in 40 studies.
elements.reason: The abstract describes how results were synthesized, including the computed summary secondary attack rate estimates and prediction intervals.

elements.quote: Data synthesis: Of 927 studies identi fi ed, 80 were included.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (80). It does not provide total participants, but it does summarize key study characteristics via outcome estimates by symptom group.

elements.quote: Summary secondary attack rate estimates were 1% (95% CI 0% e 2%) with a prediction interval of 0% e 10% for asymptomatic index cases in ten studies, 7% (95% CI 3% e 11%) with a prediction interval of 1% e 40% for pre-symptomatic cases in 11 studies and 6% (95% CI 5% e 8%) with a prediction interval of 5% e 38% for symptomatic index cases in 40 studies.
elements.reason: Results for the main outcomes are reported for each symptom status group, including effect estimates and confidence intervals.

elements.quote: Summary secondary attack rate estimates were 1% (95% CI 0% e 2%) with a prediction interval of 0% e 10% for asymptomatic index cases in ten studies, 7% (95% CI 3% e 11%) with a prediction interval of 1% e 40% for pre-symptomatic cases in 11 studies and 6% (95% CI 5% e 8%) with a prediction interval of 5% e 38% for symptomatic index cases in 40 studies.
elements.reason: The abstract provides summary estimates with 95% CIs, but it does not state that a meta-analysis was conducted (the PRISMA item is conditional on that wording).

elements.quote: Conclusion: Asymptomatic patients can transmit SARS-CoV-2 to others, but our fi ndings indicate that such individuals are responsible for fewer secondary infections than people with symptoms.
elements.reason: The abstract compares groups and indicates the direction of effect (asymptomatic associated with fewer secondary infections than symptomatic).

elements.quote: Transmission Limitations: We excluded some studies because the index case or number of contacts were unclear.
elements.reason: Important limitations are briefly summarized in the abstract.

elements.quote: Conclusion: Asymptomatic patients can transmit SARS-CoV-2 to others, but our fi ndings indicate that such individuals are responsible for fewer secondary infections than people with symptoms.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results and its implication.
The provided evidence for the abstract does not report the primary source of funding.

elements.quote: Systematic review registration: PROSPERO CRD42020188168.
elements.reason: The abstract provides the register name (PROSPERO) and registration number (CRD42020188168).

elements.quote: Background: Reports suggest that asymptomatic individuals (those with no symptoms at all throughout infection) with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) are infectious, but the extent of transmission based on symptom status requires further study.
elements.reason: The abstract describes the current state of knowledge (suggested infectiousness of asymptomatic individuals) and an important uncertainty (extent of transmission by symptom status requires further study).

elements.quote: Purpose: This living review aims to critically appraise available data about secondary attack rates from people with asymptomatic, pre-symptomatic and symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection.
elements.reason: The need for conducting the review is explicitly explained via the stated purpose to appraise data on secondary attack rates by symptom status.
No evidence is provided about previous similar systematic reviews and how the need for the current living review is justified relative to them.
This review concerns secondary attack rates/transmission evidence rather than an intervention effect, so describing a mechanism of action for an intervention is not applicable.
The provided evidence does not indicate a complex intervention or delivery context that would require a logic model of hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes.

elements.quote: The aim of this review is to summarize the available evidence about secondary attack rates (de fi ned as the probability that an infected individual will transmit the disease to a susceptible individual) among the contacts of individuals with SARS-CoV-2 with different symptom status to provide information about how contagious they are, and their role in driving the pandemic.
elements.reason: An explicit objective/aim is stated, but it is not clearly formulated using a relevant question-formulation framework (e.g., explicitly structured question using a named framework).

elements.quote: The larger review aims to answer transmission dynamics of SARS-CoV-2. The analysis in this report addresses one of the review questions; to identify secondary attack rate based on symptom status.
elements.reason: This is not a review of intervention effects, so planned comparisons using PICO (or variant) are not applicable to the objective described.

elements.quote: Studies were eligible if they met the inclusion criteria: (a) report on COVID-19 or SARS-CoV-2 infection and (b) report an outbreak investigation or contact tracing study.
elements.reason: The evidence specifies some study characteristics for eligibility (COVID-19/SARS‑CoV‑2; outbreak investigation/contact tracing). elements.quote: Secondary attack rates were computed from raw data in each study, dividing the number of infected contacts of primary cases by the total number of susceptible exposed contacts. A pooled analysis was carried out to generate summary estimates for the secondary attack rate in each subgroup analysed (asymptomatic, pre-symptomatic and symptomatic index cases), in the framework of a random effect model. Secondary attack rates are presented as a proportion along with 95% CIs in forest plots.
elements.reason: The effect measure used for outcomes is specified as secondary attack rate, calculated as infected contacts divided by susceptible exposed contacts, and presented as a proportion with 95% confidence intervals.

elements.quote: The Freeman e Tukey double-arcsine variancestabilizing transformation was used to combine data, because of its advantage over log and logit transformations, which do not allow computation of the proportion in the presence of zero event counts [15]. Secondary attack rates are presented as a proportion along with 95% CIs in forest plots.
elements.reason: There is a rationale for using a specific transformation to combine proportion data with zero events, but the retrieved evidence does not explicitly justify the overall choice of the effect measure itself beyond presenting secondary attack rates as proportions.

elements.quote: Studies were eligible if they met the inclusion criteria: (a) report on COVID-19 or SARS-CoV-2 infection and (b) report an outbreak investigation or contact tracing study. Exclusion criteria were: (a) review articles; (b) observational studies providing only the proportion of individuals infected; (c) studies that do not indicate the number of contacts or secondary infections; and (d) reports in media sources. We also manually screened the references of the included original studies and reviews to identify additional eligible studies.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes inclusion/exclusion criteria and an additional screening step (reference checking), but the evidence provided does not specify the processes used to decide eligibility for each synthesis/each planned subgroup in terms of comparing against planned groups for each synthesis.

elements.quote: These fi ndings suggest that individuals who are asymptomatic throughout the disease course are responsible for fewer secondary infections than symptomatic and presymptomatic cases. Most transmission events were associated with living with the index case or group activities such as sharing meals and playing board games. Given the importance of transmission heterogeneity in propagating the pandemic, it is important that we learn about the various factors that contribute to transmission. According to modelling and contact tracing studies, around 80% of secondary infections can be linked to 20% of cases, which distinguishes SARS-CoV-2 from seasonal in fl uenza, although a similar pattern was also observed in SARS-CoV and Middle East respiratory syndrome-CoV [82 e 84].
elements.reason: The discussion interprets the review’s findings and explicitly relates them to other evidence, including modelling and contact tracing studies and comparisons to other pathogens.
